subtopics.title: Where People Are — Distribution, Density and Why

questions.question: Population distribution and population density differ in that:
options: Distribution describes the pattern of where people are; density measures how many per unit of area
Distribution counts people; density describes their pattern
They are two words for the same measure
Density applies only to cities

questions.question: A region of 3 million people covering 25 000 square kilometres has a density of:
options: 83 people per square kilometre
12 people per square kilometre
120 people per square kilometre
1 200 people per square kilometre

questions.question: Australia's tiny national density misleads because:
options: Its census excludes coastal cities
Its deserts are densely settled
Its population is falling rapidly
Density is an average, and nearly all Australians actually crowd onto two coastal fringes

questions.question: Gauteng holds roughly a quarter of South Africa's population on a dry plateau because:
options: It has the country's best rainfall
The gold discoveries of 1886 pulled labour, railways and industry there — a human factor overruling physical ones
It lies on a major navigable river
Apartheid policy concentrated people there by law

subtopics.title: Growth, Structure and the Population Pyramid

questions.question: A birth rate of 24 per thousand against a death rate of 9 per thousand gives a natural increase of:
options: 33 per thousand, or 3.3 per cent
9 per thousand, or 0.9 per cent
24 per thousand, or 2.4 per cent
15 per thousand, which is 1.5 per cent per year

questions.question: In stage two of the demographic transition model, population explodes because:
options: The death rate falls with clean water, vaccines and food while the birth rate stays high
Both birth and death rates rise together
Migration doubles the population
The birth rate rises while deaths stay constant

questions.question: Overpopulation is best defined as:
options: Any population above ten million
A density above 100 people per square kilometre
More people than an area's resources can support at an acceptable standard of living — a relationship, not a count
The population of the largest city in a country

questions.question: South Africa's population pyramid carries a visible scar because:
options: Emigration emptied the elderly bars
The HIV pandemic cut into the young-adult bars and lowered life expectancy through the 2000s, before mass treatment turned it upward
A famine in the 1990s reduced births
The census stopped counting some ages

subtopics.title: People on the Move — Migration, Urbanisation and Settlement

questions.question: One person crossing a border earns two labels because they are:
options: A commuter at home and a refugee abroad
A migrant in summer and a resident in winter
An emigrant leaving their country and an immigrant entering the next
An internal migrant and then an external one

questions.question: In South Africa's internal migration, the sending regions such as the Eastern Cape and Limpopo:
options: Age and hollow as their young adults leave, sustained partly by remittances
Gain population as cities empty
Lose only their oldest residents
Are unaffected by the movement

questions.question: Urbanisation is defined as:
options: The total number of people in cities
The rising percentage of a population living in urban places — a share, not a count
The construction rate of new suburbs
The physical growth of city boundaries

questions.question: The preferred response to informal settlements is upgrading rather than removal because:
options: Removal costs nothing but takes longer
Upgrading requires no municipal spending
The settlements are temporary by nature
The settlements stand within reach of work, so services and tenure should be brought to where people already live

subtopics.title: Water in a Dry Country — Floods and Water Management

questions.question: The numbers that frame South Africa's water problem are:
options: About 465 millimetres of rain against a world average near 860, with only about 9 per cent becoming river flow
About 860 millimetres of rain with 50 per cent runoff
About 200 millimetres of rain with no runoff at all
World-average rainfall spread perfectly evenly

questions.question: On a hydrograph, a sealed urban catchment signs itself as:
options: A long lag time and a low rounded peak
No change from the rural signature
A short lag time and a tall narrow peak
A falling base flow with no peak

questions.question: The Jukskei 2022 and Natal 1987 events pair as case studies because they show:
options: Two identical regional floods
The minutes-fast urban flash flood against the days-long province-wide regional flood
Two dam failures
Floods that caused no loss of life

questions.question: A percentage point of irrigation efficiency outweighs whole suburbs of shorter showers because:
options: Farms pay more for water than households
Households cannot reduce their use
Shorter showers increase evaporation
Irrigation takes roughly 60 per cent of the nation's water, so small farm savings move huge volumes

questions.question: In the schoolyard picture, the tuckshop crush stands for:
options: Gauteng — people clustering where work is served
The Northern Cape's empty spaces
The country's coastline
The rainfall gradient

questions.question: Forty learners at the tuckshop counter and forty on the far field differ in:
options: Distribution only, never density
Total population
Density — the same number of people divided by very different areas
Neither distribution nor density

questions.question: The Northern Cape is the far field of the map because:
options: Its climate is too cold for settlement
Its land is too mountainous to farm
Mining is forbidden there
Almost no rain means almost no farming and almost no jobs, leaving about 2 people per square kilometre

questions.question: Reading the choir photograph takes three looks:
options: The front row, how fast the rows thin, and the back rows — births, survival, old age
The conductor, the hall and the song
Left side, right side and centre
Height, weight and age of each singer

questions.question: The wedge-shaped choir sings for:
options: A rich country with too few workers
A young, poor, fast-growing country with heavy youth dependency
A country with balanced age groups
A shrinking, ageing country

questions.question: Countries square off from wedge toward block because:
options: Migration removes the youngest rows
Birth rates fall before death rates do
Death rates fall first, then birth rates follow as children survive and women gain choices
Both rates rise as countries develop

subtopics.title: The Leaking Jojo Tank — South Africa's Water Story

questions.question: The three faults of the national tank are that it is:
options: Small, unpredictably filled, and leaking a third through broken pipes
Green, plastic and imported
Too large, too full and too clean
Owned by farmers, cities and mines

questions.question: Land in a city is free because something is wrong with it warns that:
options: City land is always polluted
Municipal land may not be occupied
Free land is far from all employment
Unclaimed land is often the floodplain — ground the river built and returns to claim

questions.question: Sealing suburbs under tar and draining wetlands changes the storm's arrival by:
options: Delaying the flood by several days
Shortening the lag and raising the peak, so water reaches doorsteps sooner and higher
Spreading the flood evenly across the city
Reducing total runoff to zero

questions.question: The one-sentence version of the year's human geography is:
options: Rain falls evenly, so people settle evenly
Cities grow only where rivers are dammed
People moved for work, settled on the land that was left, and the land that was left belonged to the water
Migration, settlement and water are three unrelated topics
